notes.meaning: Dinah went out on her own to visit the women living in the nearby Canaanite town. She was young and curious, but leaving the safety of her family's camp exposed her to serious danger among strangers who did not know God.
Shechem, the son of the local ruler, saw Dinah and took her by force. This was a brutal crime that brought great dishonor and pain to Dinah and Jacob's entire family.
After assaulting Dinah, Shechem fell deeply in love with her. He kept her in his home and tried to win her over by speaking kindly and comforting her.
Shechem asked his father Hamor to arrange a marriage with Dinah. In the ancient world, even among pagans, young people usually sought their parents' help and consent before getting married.

Jacob learned what had happened to Dinah, but he kept quiet and did nothing right away. He was deeply grieved, yet he waited for his grown sons to return from tending the sheep before deciding what to do.
Hamor went out from the city to talk with Jacob about the situation. He wanted to calm the family down and ask officially for Dinah's hand in marriage for his son.

Jacob's sons came home from the fields as soon as they heard the shocking news. They were filled with grief and deep anger, because violating a daughter of Jacob was an outrage against the covenant family of God.
Hamor spoke with Jacob and his sons on behalf of Shechem. He told them how much his son loved Dinah and asked them to let her become his wife.
Hamor proposed that the two groups unite through marriage. He wanted their families to freely marry one another's daughters, joining their communities together.

Hamor offered Jacob's family the right to live, trade, and buy land anywhere they wished. This sounded like a generous offer, but accepting it would mean blending in with the Canaanites and losing their separate identity as God's chosen people.
Shechem stepped forward to beg Dinah's father and brothers for their permission. He promised to give them whatever they asked if only they would agree to the marriage.
Shechem offered to pay any price or bride-gift they demanded. In those days, a bridegroom paid a bridal price to the family, and Shechem was willing to pay whatever it took to make Dinah his wife.
Jacob's sons answered Shechem and Hamor with a deceitful plan. Because their sister had been violated, they hid their true intentions and plotted revenge instead of seeking honest justice.

The brothers claimed they could never allow their sister to marry a man who was not circumcised. Circumcision was the sacred covenant sign God gave to Abraham's family, and marrying someone without it would bring disgrace on them.
The brothers made one specific condition for their agreement. They told the Canaanite leaders that every male in the town must be circumcised, just like Jacob's family.

They promised that if the men complied, the two groups would freely intermarry and become one united people. The brothers used this promise of total unity as a trap, having no real intention of keeping it.
The brothers warned that if the men refused circumcision, they would take Dinah and leave immediately. This gave Hamor and Shechem the impression that there was no room for bargaining.
Hamor and Shechem were pleased with the proposal and quickly accepted the condition. Hamor wanted to make his son happy, and Shechem was eager to do whatever it took to win Dinah.
Shechem did not wait to follow through because he loved Dinah so deeply. He was the most respected man in his household, which helped him persuade others to follow his lead.
Hamor and Shechem went to the city gate, which was the public meeting place for community decisions and legal business. There they gathered the local citizens to present the proposal.
The leaders spoke well of Jacob's family, calling them peaceful neighbors with plenty of room in the land to share. They urged the citizens to trade with them and intermarry.

Hamor and Shechem explained that the only requirement for becoming one united people was for every male in the city to be circumcised. They made it sound like a simple condition for a great partnership.
The leaders appealed to the people's greed by pointing out Jacob's vast wealth. They promised that the family's livestock and goods would eventually belong to the city if they joined together.
The men of the city agreed to the plan out of loyalty to their rulers and the hope of financial gain. Every male in the city went through with circumcision as proposed.

Three days later, when the men were in severe pain and fever from their surgery, Simeon and Levi attacked. Dinah's full brothers led a surprise assault and slaughtered every defenseless man in the town.
Simeon and Levi killed both Hamor and Shechem with the sword. They rescued Dinah from Shechem's house and took her back home with them.
The other sons of Jacob joined in after the killing was done and ransacked the city. They felt justified because their sister had been violated, but their actions turned into greedy plunder.
The brothers seized all the sheep, cattle, and donkeys belonging to the town. They took everything they could find, both inside the town walls and out in the surrounding fields.
The brothers captured the women and children and carried away all the wealth from the houses. What began as a defense of family honor turned into total destruction and theft.

Jacob rebuked Simeon and Levi for putting the whole family in terrible danger. He feared that the surrounding Canaanites would unite to wipe them out, because they were few in number and now hated by everyone.
Simeon and Levi showed no regret and angrily defended what they had done. They asked their father if they were supposed to sit by and let their sister be treated like a prostitute.
